blocks.text: In 1952 the American biologists Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase did experiments to confirm that DNA is the genetic material, using bacteriophages, viruses that attack bacteria.

Background: a bacteriophage has a core of DNA or RNA and a protein coat. A lytic phage binds to the surface of a bacterium and injects some material into the cell; this material is hereditary, because it directs the making of new phages inside the bacterium, which finally bursts (lyses) and releases them. The question was which material, nucleic acid or protein or both, the phage injects.

items: They used a phage containing DNA, not RNA, and labelled its parts with different radioactive isotopes as tracers.
Some phages were grown with sulphur-35 (35S), which entered the amino acids of the protein coats; others with phosphorus-32 (32P), which entered the phosphate groups of the DNA.
Setup 1: phages with 35S-labelled protein infected bacteria. Setup 2: phages with 32P-labelled DNA infected bacteria.
After some time the infected cells and the medium were separated by centrifugation and tested for radioactivity.

blocks.caption: Results
rows: the medium, not the bacterial cells
the bacterial cells, not the medium

blocks.text: So during infection the 32P-labelled DNA entered the bacterial cells and directed the making of new phages, while the 35S-labelled protein coat stayed outside. Hershey and Chase concluded that the phage DNA, not the protein, directs the production of new phages.

blocks.alt: Two setups. Setup 1, radioactive sulphur (35S): phages with radioactive protein coats and normal DNA infect bacteria; after the blender and centrifugation the radioactivity is in the virus proteins in the medium and there is no radioactivity in the bacterial cells. Setup 2, radioactive phosphorus (32P): phages with radioactive DNA infect bacteria; after the blender and centrifugation the radioactivity is in the virus DNA inside the bacterial cells.
